body.text: How can artificial intelligence help small firms become more productive and transform economies? Behind this question is the hope that AI will do for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) what decades of credit schemes and training programmes have struggled to achieve. MSMEs, generally defined as establishments employing 250 or fewer workers, make up over 97 per cent of enterprises in ASEAN and around 85 per cent of employment. Indonesia alone has some 65 million MSMEs employing about 119 million people.

Technology alone rarely transforms an economy; its benefits depend on the surrounding institutions, skills and business relationships. These constraints apply to AI as well. Countries need credible data, capable workers, and adequate financing and market demand to realise the potential productivity gains of AI’s powerful technology.

Around 1900, American factories began replacing steam engines with electric motors powered by central dynamos, yet productivity barely moved for two decades. As Paul David showed in his study of the “dynamo paradox”, the gains came in the 1920s, when factories were redesigned around electricity: electric machines were placed where the production flow needed them, and work was organised differently.

With AI, many MSMEs are at a stage comparable to factories in the early 1900s. Adding a tool to an unchanged production workflow changes little. The OECD has found that even in its member countries, mostly high-income economies, about half of SMEs remain at basic or developing levels of digital maturity, and only one in five uses AI at an advanced or transformative level. Many Southeast Asian firms still lack the foundations: production data, connected processes and AI-proficient managers.

Industrial adoption is also more complex and difficult than consumer adoption, as an ADB Report notes. Anyone can use a new app within minutes. However, a workshop using AI to detect product defects needs consistent images, agreed inspection criteria, trained workers and a clear response when the system flags an issue. These integration and maintenance costs hit small firms hardest, strengthening the case for public support.
For MSMEs, however, redesign cannot stop at the factory gate. Small firms cannot develop capabilities alone; they depend on lenders, technical centres, suppliers and buyers.

Middle-income Asia-Pacific economies, including most ASEAN members, match the global frontier on access to electricity but are far behind on research capacity, export diversification, renewables and finance.

UNIDO’s Industrial Development Report 2026 shows the scale of gaps that hinder productivity-boosting AI integration. Middle-income Asia-Pacific economies, including most ASEAN members, match the global frontier on access to electricity but are far behind on research capacity, export diversification, renewables and finance. For a small manufacturer, these gaps compound; a capable entrepreneur with a good product can still be stopped by scarce credit, weak technical services or an inability to prove quality to a buyer.

Brynjolfsson, Rock and Syverson describe a productivity J-curve: investment in new technologies initially requires complementary organisational changes and intangible assets, whose benefits may not immediately appear in measured productivity. Large firms can finance this transition, but cash-constrained MSMEs often cannot. Pilot projects may demonstrate what a technology can achieve, yet funding frequently ends before firms have reorganised production, trained workers and secured commercial demand. The result is a “pilot-to-scale trap” that forestalls projects — even promising ones — before they become commercially sustainable.

Large “lead” firms, with government support, can foster MSME development and upgrade, as observed in Japan’s keiretsu networks and Korea’s large industrial groups. Their remarkable success stemmed from productive linkages between larger firms and MSMEs within a conglomerate or supply chain, together with high operational standards, disciplined commercial terms and supportive public policy that significantly redesigned the enterprise ecosystem (Table 1). The Japanese and Korean industrialisation experience, and its contrasts with other countries’ track record of weak or extractive linkages, offer contemporary lessons for building enterprise capabilities in all sectors, including AI. The broad principles would apply in general, although the extent to which this approach can be adopted would depend on country conditions and the presence of large firms.
Table 1. MSME development through large-firm and public-sector linkages

AI can strengthen MSME productivity but cannot replace public policy instruments and lead firms, particularly in the manufacturing and tradable sectors. Indeed, Southeast Asian industrial policies are strengthening laboratories, metrology, accreditation and certification along export value chains, from seaweed in Indonesia to fruit in Vietnam and fish in Cambodia, so that small producers’ test results are accepted abroad. Another public-private instrument is eco-industrial parks, which, by sharing infrastructure, common services and resource exchanges, such as using one firm’s waste or by-products as another’s input, lighten the load on each firm. Well-managed parks can become shared service platforms, extending technical services and infrastructure to MSMEs beyond their boundaries.
To continue industrialisation while integrating AI, ASEAN countries should uphold three priorities in developing MSMEs, especially in manufacturing and international trade.
First, release the constraints that block a good ecosystem. Tie support for digital adoption and AI to process redesign and skills, since most MSMEs cannot reorganise production systems on their own.

Second, finance the redesign of production processes, not only AI technology adoption. Well-designed financial and technical assistance should carry firms through the early and difficult stages of the J-curve so that projects are sustained until they can take off. These efforts should involve intermediaries such as industry associations, technical centres and industrial parks to expand the benefits of positive spillovers.

Third, redesign the production process based on the buyer requirements. Start with what markets demand in quality, standards and delivery, work back to the capabilities firms need and only then, choose how to use AI technology. Through lead firms, quality infrastructure and eco-industrial parks, sustainability compliance can become a route to market access.

The factories of the past needed decades to get reorganised around electricity, and the faster movers secured footholds in the new economy. Things are moving considerably faster today; Southeast Asia should act decisively and strategically. The real test of its next generation of MSME programmes is not how many firms receive AI tools, but how many acquire the capabilities, finance and market connections to use them productively.
